name: Solus
summary: An independent, curated rolling-release Linux distribution built from scratch exclusively for modern 64-bit desktop computing, featuring the eopkg package manager and the flagship Budgie desktop.

content.introduction: Solus is an independent GNU/Linux operating system designed from scratch specifically for personal desktop computing on 64-bit x86_64 PC hardware. Established in 2014 by Ikey Doherty under the name Evolve OS and renamed Solus in 2015, the distribution is developed by a dedicated community team. Unburdened by server or enterprise legacy, Solus focuses singularly on providing a polished, fast, and responsive user experience for desktop workstations, creative workflows, and home entertainment.
content.what_is_it: Technically, Solus is a standalone distribution built without reliance on upstream repositories such as Debian, Ubuntu, or Arch Linux. It utilizes its own binary package manager, `eopkg` (an evolved derivative of Pardus's PiSi), alongside the `ypkg` build engine. Solus operates on a curated rolling-release model where software updates are tested and delivered continuously through stable weekly update rings, supplemented by periodic refresh installation ISOs.
content.origin_and_history: Solus began development in 2014 as an initiative to build a modern, non-derivative Linux desktop. In tandem with the distribution, the team created the Budgie desktop environment, which gained widespread popularity across the broader Linux ecosystem. Over a decade of development, Solus evolved its governance into an international non-profit collective, successfully navigated infrastructural transitions, implemented full UsrMerge filesystem unification, and published regular major release ISO refreshes including Solus 4.5 'Resilience', Solus 4.6 'Convergence', 4.7, 4.8, and 4.9.
content.package_management_and_eopkg: Software management in Solus is driven by `eopkg`, an adapted and modernized fork of PiSi (Packages Installed Successfully as Intended, originally developed by Pardus Linux). `eopkg` utilizes XML-based metadata and compressed archives for binary package distribution, supporting binary delta updates to reduce network bandwidth during system upgrades. Source packages are built using `ypkg`, Solus's specialized YAML-based package build tool, which ensures clean build environments and reproducible packaging. For graphical software management, Solus includes the Solus Software Center (`solus-sc`), which categorizes native applications, manages system updates, and integrates Flatpak support out of the box, granting access to thousands of sandboxed third-party applications from Flathub alongside native repositories.
content.desktop_editions_and_budgie: Solus is the ancestral home and primary showcase of the Budgie desktop environment, originally created by Ikey Doherty specifically for the distribution. Budgie combines a traditional desktop metaphor with modern visual design, featuring the Raven notification and widget side panel, customizable panel applets, and tight integration with GNOME underlying libraries. While the Budgie project has since transitioned to the independent Buddies of Budgie organization to foster cross-distribution adoption, Solus continues to offer it as its flagship edition. In addition to Budgie, Solus produces official desktop editions featuring GNOME, MATE, and XFCE, each tailored with curated themes, unified icon sets, and optimized desktop defaults.
content.hardware_support_and_focus: Solus maintains an uncompromising hardware focus strictly targeted at modern 64-bit x86 (x86-64) personal computers, intentionally foregoing server, IoT, and ARM single-board computer support. Hardware detection and proprietary driver deployment are automated by Linux Driver Management (LDM), an in-house utility that identifies NVIDIA graphics cards, Wi-Fi chipsets, and peripheral controllers, automatically configuring corresponding kernel modules and 32-bit compatibility libraries for Steam gaming. Kernel lifecycle management is handled by `clr-boot-manager` (adapted from Intel's Clear Linux), which manages kernel slots and automates systemd-boot EFI entries. Solus operates a curated rolling-release model where package updates are thoroughly tested in the unstable repository before being synchronized to the stable repository every Friday ('Sync Friday').
content.release_line_and_versioning: Solus 4.9, named Serenity, was published on 18 April 2026 by Evan Maddock and is the first release of 2026. The 4.6 notes (14 October 2024), 4.7 and 4.8 precede it in the announcement feed, which is tagged news and releases. Each release is published in four editions - Budgie, GNOME, Plasma and Xfce - and the release notes separate the changes common to all editions from those specific to each desktop.
content.system_administration_conventions: Two administrative changes are introduced in 4.9. Enabling default services now relies on systemd preset files: the project previously enabled services by creating symbolic links into `*.wants` directories, which prevented systemd from reporting service status correctly and made the setup harder to manage. The default privileged group changes from `sudo` to `wheel`, most upstream software assuming `wheel`, which removes a set of patches that had to be carried across package updates.
content.installation_encryption_and_partitioning: The 4.9 image ships GRUB 2.14 on legacy non-EFI systems, a version supporting Argon2 encryption and therefore LUKS2. The Calamares installer is updated to 3.4.2 and the Solus configuration uses its new capabilities: disk encryption moves to LUKS2, and the key can be stored in the machine's TPM so that partitions unlock automatically. The recommended default size of the EFI partition is raised to 2 GB, as firmware modules, kernel modules and NVIDIA packages keep growing in size.
content.shipped_kernel_and_desktop_stack: The release ships Linux kernel 6.18.21 and an LTS branch carrying the same version number at the time of publication; from this release onwards Solus uses the same patch set and kernel configuration as AerynOS, from which the project expects broader hardware enablement. The graphics stack is based on Mesa 26.0.4. Applications common to the four editions are Firefox 149.0.2, LibreOffice 25.8.6.2 and Thunderbird 149.0.2, and the default terminal becomes ptyxis. The desktops shipped are Budgie 10.9.4, GNOME 49.5, KDE Plasma 6.6.4 with KDE Frameworks 6.24.0 and KDE Gear 25.12.3, and Xfce 4.20; the project announces the removal of X11 support in Budgie 10.10, GNOME 50 and Plasma 6.8.
advantages: Built from scratch specifically for personal desktop computing without server compromises
Curated rolling-release model providing current software combined with weekly stability testing
Flagship Budgie desktop environment offering intuitive ergonomics and low resource overhead
High responsiveness with optimized x86_64 compiler flags and fast delta package updates via eopkg
Native Flatpak and Flathub integration in the Software Center for broad third-party application support
Dual kernel branches (current and LTS) offering tailored compatibility for both modern and legacy PC components
disadvantages: Strictly limited to 64-bit x86_64 hardware, lacking official ARM64 single-board computer support
Native repository catalog is smaller than immense community archives like Arch AUR or Debian/Ubuntu pools
Custom eopkg package manager commands require learning distinct syntax different from apt, dnf, or pacman
Independent developer base can result in slower triage for highly specialized enterprise or niche developer packages
who_is_it_for: Everyday desktop users and enthusiasts seeking a fast, cohesive personal workstation OS without complex configuration
Users who appreciate a rolling-release distribution that conducts weekly stabilization checks before releasing updates
Fans of the Budgie desktop environment desiring the most authentic and integrated Budgie experience
who_is_it_not_for: System administrators managing headless servers, cloud container nodes, or virtualization hypervisors
Users operating ARM single-board computers (Raspberry Pi) or legacy 32-bit machines
Specialized developers requiring esoteric scientific libraries absent from native repositories or Flatpak
content.verdict: Solus is an independent desktop-oriented Linux distribution engineered without upstream packaging inheritance. By pairing its custom eopkg package manager with native Budgie, GNOME, and Xfce desktop editions, curated Friday repository synchronizations, and automated driver tooling, it provides an accessible and coherent workstation environment tailored specifically for x86-64 personal computing.
